title: The wish Prahlada refused
hookLine: offered any wish at all, a boy says no thanks
carry: bhakti asks nothing, yet every asker is welcome
tomorrow: one wish, then. and the boy spends it on someone else. who?
last: THE DOORWAY. THE DUSK. THE LAP.

lines: EVEN THE GODS WON'T GO NEAR.
cards: A genie, a wishing well, birthday candles: there are plenty of stories about getting a wish. Here's one where a boy turns it down.

Narasimha is still raging in the hall, and in the Bhagavata, even the gods won't go near him. So Brahma sends the one person who isn't afraid: Prahlada. The boy walks up and bows, and the lion grows calm.
Ask me for anything, he says. And Prahlada says: I'd rather not.

teach.b: Prahlada explains, and this is bhakti, devotion, at its height. Someone who serves in order to get rewards, he says, isn't a servant. He's a trader, doing business.
So he asks for one thing only: that no wanting would rise in his heart at all. Here's that view at its strongest.
Love that keeps a receipt isn't quite love. If you only call your grandmother when you need money, she can tell. Prahlada wants a relationship, not a transaction.
Now the other view, and it comes from inside the tradition too.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names four kinds of people who turn to him: the one in trouble, the one who wants to understand, the one who wants something, and the wise. And he calls all four of them noble.
Here's that view at its strongest. A prayer can start in a hard place: a hospital waiting room, a lost job, a test you might fail. The Gita doesn't send that person away for asking.
The asking is how the door opens. So which is it? The tradition keeps both.
Prahlada's no thanks is honored as the high road. Krishna's welcome keeps the road open for everyone still on the way. And Narasimha doesn't settle it either.
He hears the boy out, and then he says: one wish, anyway.

how: Some Hindus pray for specific help, in hard times or before exams and journeys; others keep a practice that asks for nothing at all; some do both.

o: a wish-granting lion from a children's fable
the boon a demon king won from Brahma
Vishnu as the man-lion, who offered Prahlada a wish

games.q: two views, one boy — tap the pairs.
p: one of the four who turn to Krishna
hears him out, then: one wish anyway

s: in the tradition, asking God for things is looked down on
in the Gita, Krishna calls the one who wants something noble too.
Prahlada turns the boon down at first
someone who serves for rewards, he says, is a trader, not a servant.
the gods rush to calm Narasimha down
they keep their distance. Brahma sends a child.

games.q: a friend only prays when things go wrong, and feels like a fake for it. which answer gives both views their due?
o: Krishna calls the one in trouble noble; Prahlada shows where asking can grow.
she's right to feel fake; Prahlada says asking turns prayer into trading.
it doesn't matter either way; the tradition has nothing to say about asking.
games.why: the Gita welcomes the one who turns to Krishna in trouble. Prahlada's no thanks is honored as the high road, not a door shut on the askers.

practice: If you have paper, write two short lines, or just make them in your head. On the first, one thing you'd ask for today. On the second, one thing you love that you'd keep loving even if nothing came of it.
Sit with both; the tradition keeps room for each.

wordCard.voice: Narasimha: the man-lion who, calm at last, offered a child anything, and heard him say he'd rather have nothing.

orig.note: Sanskrit: noble, generous. Krishna's word in the Gita for all four kinds who turn to him.

carryVoice: Keep this one: bhakti at its height asks for nothing, and Krishna still calls every asker noble. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 7.9 (no one dares approach the raging Narasimha; Brahma sends Prahlada; the lion is calmed)
Bhagavata Purana 7.10.1–7 (the boon offered; one who serves for rewards is a trader, not a servant; Prahlada asks that no desire arise in his heart)
Bhagavad Gita 7.16–18 (four kinds turn to Krishna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of gain, the wise; all are noble)
